doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Race, family and the younger generation
title: Today's young people, rappers and their forefathers
summary: Hamilton complains that young people and rappers do not know what their forefathers went through, and he describes teens on the bus.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Okay, let’s bring it on into the ‘60s. Now that we’ve set the stage and we know where -­

Okay, but you understand where I’m coming from? I’m not the great I am or anything. I’m not the only dude that’s -- you know, it’s like the younger generation man, they have an opportunity -- that’s one of the things that bothers me, just like it bothers Sharpton, Jessie Jackson, all those guys.

I can’t get with these young dudes that want to refer to, whore this -- the rappers. They have no idea, man. They have no idea what their forefathers went through to get to where they are now, you dig? You know?
A lot of them don’t have fathers.

That’s beside the point. That’s beside the point, man. Poverty is a state of mind. You don’t have to be poor, man. You don’t have to be poor, man. You can get more with a thank you and a gun then you can -­
I like that, and a gun. That’s a big qualifier there. As opposed to a -- you get a thank you and a gun as opposed to -- please complete that statement, Mr. Hamilton.
That was it, right. Enough said.

But anyway, it’s my daughter’s generation. Her offspring. They’re the ones ­ - and man opportunities -- man, have you any idea how much money these rappers make? If I ever made that kind of money, man, it would be just bull, you know. And really from what I can see in here, it’s nothing but bull. And the young white people, guys, girls, they ain’t no different.

Hey man, let me tell you something. Let me tell you, when I catch the bus coming home, sometimes I come across town. I’m on 14th and 6th Avenue. I come across town to 1st Avenue. I get on the bus and all of these kids, Catholic with the uniforms on, girls, get on the bus, right? I’m sitting down, right, there’s about two or three of them standing right behind me, right, conversation, of this m-f -- white girls.
That’s a heck of a qualifier there.

This is the truth, man. I didn’t believe, you know. I don’t know whether they know what the word means, they’re just -- you know, it’s talk. But this, you know, that’s what you’re into now, man. Don’t you have it out your way?
